newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU leaders to meet on bloc's future.
newsitem.headline: EU leaders to meet on bloc's future.

text.p: Western Europe's leaders, worried about how the European Union will cope with more than three dozen members, meet in Dublin next weekend to inject some urgency into the bloc's preparations for the 21th century.
At a summit on Saturday that many of the participants would rather not have, EU leaders will discuss the future and underline the need to hasten talks on a new EU treaty.
"What I expect to come out of it is a sense of determination and a strong sense of urgency from the (leaders)," Dutch European Affairs Minister Michiel Patijn said.
At issue is the progress of the so-called inter-governmental conference (IGC), designed to change the EU's treaty so that it can work with an influx of new members.
The EU has told 12 countries, from Estonia to eastern Europe and Malta, that they can eventually become members. Formal membership negotiations are expected to begin six months after the IGC ends.
But critics recently said treaty talks are bogged down in technocratic debates in which nations simply list their wishes.
The agenda, by comparion with previous IGCs when the single currency and moves to joint foreign policy were agreed, is also very low key, focusing mainly on internal procedures.

"A lack of dynamism, ambitions pitched too low -- those are the impressions given by the discussions at the moment," European Commission President Jacques Santer told the European Parliament earlier in the month.

Some officials are predicting that the talks will not finish as planned at the end of the Dutch EU presidency next June, but will stretch on into the Luxembourg presidency which follows -- delaying the beginning of enlargement talks.

Negotiators themselves said talks are going as well as could be expected given that most countries are unwilling to show their hand until the final round of trade-offs which normally accompanies such treaty rewrites.

But even some of those deeply involved in the negotiations say there is an unwillingness among the EU governments to take the tough decisions on power sharing needed to prepare the bloc for enlargement.
"Everybody understands the challenges, but no one is assuming the consequences," said one official.
The Dublin summit is supposed to give some impetus to the talks, but even here EU diplomats say most countries were less than enthusiastic about having it so soon into the negotiations.
British Prime Minister John Major, for one, will have to tread a fine line, meeting on Europe's future just days before the annual conference of his increasingly Euro-sceptic Conservative Party.

But others were also reluctant to meet only about six months into the delicate talks. There is fear, officials say, that the summit will either raise expectations or will give the impression of a crisis where one does not exist.

The summit was called by French President Jacques Chirac at the EU leaders' last meeting in Florence. Chirac is said to be concerned that if the IGC drags on, the controversial treaty ratification that follows it will bump into French elections.
For now, however, most of those involved hope the summit will focus the bloc's minds on what needs to be done.

"Do we still agree on the political objectives? Do we still agree on the role the (IGC) plays in the larger political and institutional decisions that have to be taken," Patijn, the Dutch minister, said of the questions before the leaders.
